To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(i) the proposed semantics is fully abstract for Object-Z classes and (ii) the semantics can be used to prove the equivalence of Object-Z classes.

• the semantics of classes is given by a set of labelled transition systems, where the labels represent the messages that can be sent to objects; • the semantics of an object is given by a labelled transition system, where the labels are the messages that can occur at the interface of the object and the transitions represent the behaviour of the object;
(i) the semantics of classes is based on a process model, and that (ii) this process model is a conservative extension of CSP.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following question: How can a fully abstract semantics for Object-Z classes be developed?
providing the basis for a fully formal semantics of Object-Z, and hence a formal foundation for the use of Object-Z in the specification of concurrent systems.
the definition of a fully abstract semantics and the investigation of its computational properties.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

our semantics is a fully abstract semantics in the sense that it is a bisimulation semantics, and it is also a full abstraction in the sense that the behavioural equivalence induced by our semantics is exactly the one defined by CSP.

the Object-Z semantics is a fully abstract semantics which is based on a process model which is stronger than CSP, weaker than CCS and, therefore, more appropriate for the specification and verification of reactive systems.
the semantics presented here is the strongest possible semantics of Object-Z that is still fully abstract.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a formal semantics for Object-Z which is based on the process algebra CSP, but which is not limited to the behavioural properties of CSP.
we have developed a formal framework for the specification of object oriented systems, which includes an operational model, a denotational semantics and a fully abstract semantics.
we have provided the first fully abstract semantics of object oriented classes.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the behavioural semantics of classes can be defined in a way that is independent of their implementation, and that the behavioural equivalence of classes is independent of the choice of implementation.
the Object-Z semantics of classes can be given in terms of the Object-Z semantics for individual objects.
the semantics of classes can be described without resorting to a notion of internal behaviour.
